analysis.one_liner: Taxes investment managers' carried interest as regular income instead of at low capital-gains rates.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Finance Committee before the Congress ended on Jan. 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Fund managers at private equity, hedge fund, and venture capital firms are paid largely through "carried interest" — a share of their investors' profits. Today that pay is taxed at the low capital-gains rate, roughly half the top rate on work income, even though the managers are performing a service for a fee. This bill would reclassify those profits as ordinary income, tax them at normal rates, and also apply self-employment tax, while letting genuine investors keep capital-gains treatment on their own money.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who currently make up the difference when the highest earners pay investment rates on what is essentially labor income. The additional federal revenue reduces deficits or funds programs without raising taxes on anyone else. Working fund employees who receive small carried-interest stakes would also face less of a gap between their pay and a CEO's.

how_it_helps.text: The bill treats the net capital gain allocated to an investment services partnership interest as ordinary income, ending the special capital-gains rate for carried interest [S2].

It also treats gains from selling such interests as ordinary income, and prevents tax avoidance through gifts, death transfers, and mergers, by applying income-in-respect-of-a-decedent and related rules [S2].
Carried interest income would count as net earnings from self-employment, so managers pay Medicare (and Social Security up to the cap) taxes on it, the same as other workers pay on their wages [S2].

Genuine capital is preserved: real money a manager invests alongside investors remains a "qualified capital interest" and keeps capital-gains treatment, and the bill keeps the treatment for domestic C corporations [S2].
The bill adds anti-abuse rules, including a 40 percent penalty on underpayments tied to avoidance schemes and expanded rules for tiered partnerships and publicly traded structures [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Private equity, hedge fund, and venture capital managers, plus real estate investment managers, whose largest source of pay would shift from the ~20% capital-gains rate to ordinary income rates of up to 37%, plus self-employment taxes. Their investors could face modestly lower returns, and a 10-year transition for certain publicly traded partnerships limits how fast one revenue stream changes [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity and hedge fund managers

drawbacks.text: A good-faith objection is that capital-gains rates exist to reward long-term investment, and carried interest is tied to multi-year gains on investors' assets; taxing it as salary could, in critics' view, blunt risk-taking in startups and buyouts, though the bill leaves true investors' own capital untouched [S2].

The rules are complex — definitions of investment partnerships, qualified capital interests, family partnerships, and SPAC provisions span many pages — which raises compliance and litigation costs even for firms acting in good faith [S2].

The bill applies to taxable years ending after enactment but includes transition relief, and certain publicly traded partnership income does not change for 10 years after enactment, delaying some of the revenue [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tax benefit goes overwhelmingly to a small, very high-income group — the top carried-interest earners are concentrated among the wealthiest households — while the ordinary-income treatment matches how every other service worker's pay is taxed. The main real cost is added complexity and the argument about investment incentives, softened by the bill's carve-out for genuine invested capital. On balance the change brings labor income taxed as labor income.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2024, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Tammy Baldwin introduced S. 4123 on April 15, 2024, with 15 Senate cosponsors [S4].
Its only congressional action was referral to the Senate Finance Committee; the committee never acted on it, and it received no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended Jan. 3, 2025 [S4].
All 15 cosponsors were Senate Democrats or allied independents, including Sen. Joe Manchin, and no Republican cosponsored [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity, hedge fund, and venture capital managers keep the carried-interest tax break. Taxpayers continue to absorb the revenue the bill would have raised, and no senator had to vote against it on the record.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private equity and hedge fund managers

for.name: Tammy Baldwin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Carried Interest Fairness Act of 2024 in the Senate.

for.name: 14 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 4 Senate independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Manchin, Brown, Whitehouse, Warren, Klobuchar, and Sanders.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Democrat or allied independent; no Republican signed on, and no senator ever cast a vote on the bill, so the floor split was never recorded.

industries.industry: Private equity, hedge fund, and venture capital fund managers
industries.note: Their core pay mechanism — carried interest taxed at capital-gains rates — would be converted to ordinary income plus self-employment tax, typically nearly doubling the tax rate on their largest income stream. That gap is paid for in higher taxes or deficits borne by everyone else.
Rental and investment real estate is a specified asset under the bill, so real estate carried interest would also be taxed as ordinary income.
Promote-style interests in special purpose acquisition companies would be treated as ordinary income, closing a structure sponsors use to defer and discount their gains.
The bill's complexity would create large compliance and planning work, an economic cost to taxpayers but a business gain for advisors.
